description: Share of population younger than 5 and older than 60 (or local elderly threshold). These age groups are typically more sensitive to disasters and heat.
Share of agriculture (and related primary production) in local GDP or employment, indicating economic dependence on climate-sensitive sectors.
Number of agricultural establishments (farms) per unit area. Higher densities of smallholders often imply greater exposure of food systems to drought and flood.
Share or absolute area of the study unit dedicated to agriculture.
Areas of global conservation importance based on three main attributes of conserving biodiversity, carbon and water assets under different area-based conservation targets

The Biodiversity Intactness Index (BII) measures biodiversity change using abundance data on plants, fungi and animals worldwide. The Index shows how local terrestrial biodiversity responds to human pressures such as land use change and intensification.
Incidence or count of climate-sensitive disease cases in the study area (from national/local health surveillance systems).
Dependence of local agriculture on large-scale irrigation, combining irrigated area share and irrigation water demand relative to total water use.
Electricity consumers and/or consumption intensity in the study area. Higher dependence on electricity increases sensitivity to drought- and heat-driven supply disruptions.

Multidimensional energy poverty: physical access to energy, ownership of essential energy-using appliances, and ability to afford energy services. Can be derived from census/survey indicators adapted to each country.

Modeled flood susceptibility from hydrology and terrain (e.g. elevation, slope, flow accumulation, distance to rivers), land cover, and extreme rainfall indices (e.g. Rx1day, Rx5day), optionally combined with inundation depth/extent products.
This information is the result of the composition of the indicators: low production of basic foods and lack of diversification of local production.
Forests minimize the soil erosion as tree crowns provide a surface cover which is able to reduce rainfall kinetic energy by intercepting precipitation
Recent reduction of forest or native vegetation cover within the study area.

description: Composite access to health and basic services (e.g. vaccination coverage, primary-care outcomes, infant mortality, malnutrition, piped water, adequate sanitation). Operationalize with local census/health statistics.
Density or accessibility of health facilities (hospitals, clinics) relative to population in the study area.

Count or share of households located in mapped hazard-prone zones (e.g. floodplains, landslide-susceptible slopes). Country-specific risk inventories or building footprints intersected with hazard layers can operationalize this indicator.
Basic sanitation has a direct impact on public health. A population with widespread access to water, sanitation and waste collection is less susceptible to disease.
Share of population without reliable access to safe drinking water. Limited water access increases drought and disease impacts.

Total annual precipitation considering days in which 95% of the rainfall is greater than or equal to 1.0 millimeter. Indicates precipitation of extreme intensity. The indicator is the result of multiplying the total annual precipitation above the 95th percentile and the weight assigned by experts considering its relative importance to the problem of heavy rainfall.

Share of households or population with regular solid-waste collection. Poor waste services increase public-health sensitivity to climate hazards.
Composite water-security measure covering availability, access, and risk to water uses (adapt with national or global water-security frameworks).
